title: Sindbad the Sailor: Fifth Voyage
paragraphs: Even all I had been through could not make me content with a quiet life. I soon grew tired of its pleasures and longed for change and adventure. So I set out once more, but this time in a ship of my own, which I built and fitted out at the nearest seaport. I wanted to be free to call at any port I liked and to take my time, but since I did not mean to carry enough goods to fill the hold, I invited several merchants of different nations to sail with me. We left with the first favorable wind, and after a long voyage on the open sea we landed on an unknown island, which turned out to be uninhabited. We decided to explore it anyway, but we had not gone far when we found a roc’s egg, as big as the one I had seen before and clearly almost ready to hatch, for the young bird’s beak had already broken through the shell. Whatever I said to stop them, the merchants with me fell on it with their hatchets, smashing the shell and killing the young roc. Then they lit a fire on the ground, hacked pieces off the bird and began to roast them, while I stood by in horror.

They had hardly finished their ill-omened meal when the sky above us was darkened by two huge shadows. The captain of my ship knew from experience what this meant, and he called out to us that the parent birds were coming and urged us to get on board as fast as we could. We did so and the sails were raised, but before we had gone any distance the rocs reached their plundered nest and circled over it, shrieking horribly when they found the mangled remains of their young one. For a moment we lost sight of them and were comforting ourselves that we had got away, when they reappeared and rose into the air right above our ship, and we saw that each one held an enormous rock in its claws, ready to crush us. There was a moment of breathless waiting. Then one bird let go, and the huge block of stone came hurtling through the air, but thanks to the quick thinking of the helmsman, who swung our ship sharply to one side, it fell into the sea right beside us, splitting the water so deep that we could nearly see the bottom. We had barely time to draw a breath of relief before the other rock came down with a mighty crash in the very middle of our unlucky ship, smashing it into a thousand pieces and crushing the passengers and crew or throwing them into the sea. I went down with the rest, but I was lucky enough to come up unhurt, and by holding a piece of driftwood with one hand and swimming with the other I kept myself afloat until the tide washed me up on an island. Its shores were steep and rocky, but I climbed up safely and threw myself down to rest on the green turf.

Once I had got some strength back, I started looking around the place where I had ended up, and it seemed to me a garden of delights. Trees stood everywhere, heavy with flowers and fruit, and a clear stream wound in and out of their shade. At nightfall I slept soundly in a snug hollow. Still, the thought that I was alone in a foreign land kept jolting me awake to stare around in fear, and at those moments I wished with all my heart that I had stayed comfortably at home. But the morning sun gave me back my courage, and I went wandering among the trees again, though always uneasy about what I might come across next. I had gone some way into the island when I saw an old man sitting on the river bank, bent over and frail, and at first I took him for a fellow shipwreck survivor. I went up and greeted him kindly, but all he did was nod. I asked what he was doing there, and he made signs that he wanted to cross the river to pick fruit, and seemed to be begging me to carry him on my back. I felt sorry for his age and weakness, so I lifted him up and waded across the stream. At the far bank I stooped so he could get off easily and told him to climb down. But instead of letting me set him on his feet (even now I laugh to think of it!), this creature who had looked so decrepit sprang lightly onto my shoulders, hooked his legs around my neck and squeezed so tightly that I nearly choked, and I was so terrified that I fell senseless to the ground. When I came to, my enemy was still sitting there, though he had loosened his grip just enough for me to breathe. As soon as he saw me stir, he poked me cleverly, first with one foot and then the other, until I was forced to get up and stagger around under the trees with him on my back while he picked and ate the best of the fruit. This went on all day. Even at night, when I threw myself down half dead from exhaustion, the dreadful old man kept hold of my neck, and at the first glimmer of morning he drummed on me with his heels until I had to wake and drag myself on again, my heart full of rage and bitterness.

One day I walked past a tree with several dry gourds lying beneath it. I picked one up and, to amuse myself, hollowed it out and squeezed into it the juice of several bunches of grapes, which hung from every bush. When it was full I left it wedged in the fork of a tree. A few days later, as I was carrying that hateful old man past the spot, I grabbed my gourd and had the pleasure of drinking some excellent wine, so good and so refreshing that I forgot all about my awful burden and began to sing and dance about.

The old monster quickly noticed what the drink had done to me, and that I was carrying him more lightly than usual. He reached out a bony hand and took the gourd, tasted it carefully at first, and then drained it down to the last drop. The wine was strong and the gourd was large, so he too began to sing, after a fashion, and soon I had the joy of feeling the iron grip of his goblin legs go slack. With one great effort I flung him to the ground, and he never moved again. I was so happy to be finally free of this uncanny old man that I ran leaping and bounding down to the shore. By the greatest good luck, I found some sailors there whose ship was anchored off the island so they could enjoy the delicious fruit and refill their water supply.

They listened to the story of my escape in amazement. “You fell into the hands of the Old Man of the Sea,” they said, “and it is a mercy he did not strangle you, as he has everyone else whose shoulders he has managed to climb onto. This island is famous for his evil deeds, and no merchant or sailor who lands here likes to wander far from his companions.” After we had talked for a while, they took me back with them on board their ship, where the captain welcomed me kindly. We soon set sail, and after several days we reached a large, prosperous-looking town where every house was built of stone. We anchored there, and one of the merchants, who had been very friendly to me during the voyage, took me ashore with him and showed me a lodging kept for foreign merchants. Then he gave me a large sack and pointed out a group of other men who each had one like it.
“Go with them,” he said, “and do what they do. But take care never to lose sight of them, because if you wander off, your life will be in danger.”

He gave me some provisions, said goodbye, and I set off with my new companions. I soon learned that our task was to fill our sacks with coconuts. But when I finally saw the trees, so enormously tall, with slender trunks too smooth to climb, I had no idea how we were going to manage it. The tops of the coconut palms were swarming with monkeys, big and small, leaping from tree to tree with astonishing agility. They seemed curious about us and upset by our arrival. I was surprised, at first, when my companions collected stones and started throwing them at these lively creatures, which looked harmless to me. But I soon saw the reason and joined in eagerly. The monkeys grew angry, and to pay us back in kind they began tearing nuts off the trees and hurling them at us with furious, spiteful gestures. So with very little effort our sacks were full of fruit that we could never have got any other way.

As soon as we had gathered all we could carry, we went back to the town. There my friend bought my share and advised me to keep up the same work until I had earned enough to get home. I did, and before long I had saved a fair amount. Just then I heard that a trading ship was about to sail. I said goodbye to my friend and boarded it, taking a good supply of coconuts with me. We sailed first to the islands where pepper grows, and then to Comari, where the best aloes wood is found and where, by a law that never changes, no one drinks wine. There I traded my coconuts for pepper and good aloes wood, and I went pearl fishing with some of the other merchants. My divers were so lucky that I soon had a huge number of pearls, large and perfect ones. I came back to Baghdad, delighted, with all these treasures, and sold them for large sums of money. As before, I did not forget to give a tenth of it to the poor. After that I rested from my labors and enjoyed every pleasure my wealth could buy.
When Sindbad had finished his story, he ordered that one hundred sequins be given to Hindbad, and the guests left. But after the next day’s feast he began the account of his sixth voyage, like this.
